column5: finite lifespan, toil and swift passing
column6: The psalm numbers a human life at seventy or eighty years, marked by toil, then says it passes quickly; this develops the commentary's time-as-principal image into a lifespan.

column5: עמל (table sound correspondence; unverified)
column6: The commentary's neighboring وَعَمِلُوا۟ names good action; this verse says human years are עָמָל and trouble before they fly away. The table's Arabic ع م ل–Hebrew עמל correspondence is unverified, while the shared labor context is explicit.

column5: wealth cannot follow its owner in death
column6: The rich person takes nothing when he dies and his glory does not descend after him; this matches the commentary's claim that accumulated capital cannot save the person who spent it.

column5: nothing carried from birth or toil
column6: A person leaves as naked as he came and cannot take the fruit of his labor; this supplies a direct account of worldly gain failing at death.

column5: stop striving to acquire wealth
column6: Proverbs warns against wearing oneself out to get rich; this directly questions the commentary's merchant-like pursuit of gain as a use of finite human time.

column5: wealth grows wings and vanishes
column6: The wealth a person fixes his eyes on suddenly makes wings and flies away; the image makes visible the commentary's principal that disappears despite apparent accumulation.

column5: unjust wealth abandoned midlife
column6: One who gains wealth unjustly is likened to a bird hatching what it did not lay and will leave it in midlife; this joins fraudulent gain to the loss of the person who thought it secure.

column5: riches fail on the day of wrath
column6: Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; this contrasts market capital with what can answer at final judgment.

column5: God weighs deeds
column6: Hannah says the Lord is a God of knowledge and actions are weighed by him; this links the commentary's unseen human account to divine assessment.

column5: balances belong to the Lord
column6: The verse says just balances and weights are the Lord's work; this joins the commentary's fair market scale to divine order and judgment.

column5: wicked stores and short measure
column6: Micah asks whether wicked treasure remains in a house with a scant measure; the prophet links stored wealth to the short measure that the commentary describes as stealing another's principal.

column5: false balances under divine judgment
column6: The Lord asks whether he can acquit someone with wicked scales and deceptive weights; this makes the dishonest trader's reduced measure answerable to judgment.

column5: worker longs for shade and wages
column6: Job compares the sufferer to a slave longing for shade and a hired worker waiting for wages; this continues the commentary's connection between human time, labor and its due.

column5: months of emptiness appointed
column6: Job says months of emptiness and nights of misery have been allotted to him; the verse gives a concrete example of living inside loss as an extended condition.

column5: a person's allotted day as a hireling's
column6: Job asks God to turn away until a person's day, like that of a hired worker, is complete; this links the commentary's due term to the end of labor and life.

column5: righteous and wicked share one fate
column6: Qohelet says the same event happens to righteous and wicked alike; this counters the commentary's exception group at the level of earthly outcomes, without directly addressing its afterlife account.

column5: fruitful tree that does not wither
column6: The righteous person is a tree bearing fruit in season whose leaf does not wither; this contrasts the commentary's crop lost to a destructive wind with a life that remains productive.

column5: wicked as windblown chaff
column6: The wicked are like chaff driven away by wind; this gives a scriptural contrast between the fruitful life and the commentary's image of a life's produce swept away.

column5: fruitless tree cut down and burned
column6: Jesus says a tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this joins the commentary's produce imagery to judgment based on what a life yields.

column5: account for every careless word
column6: Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this makes the commentary's comprehensive human reckoning concrete down to speech.

column5: dead judged from books by their works
column6: At the great throne, the dead are judged from opened books according to their works; this is a direct image of the final account that the commentary hears behind loss and deeds.

column5: death followed by judgment
column6: The verse says humans die once and afterward face judgment; it fits the commentary's image of each person reaching a fixed term and being assessed.

column5: postmortem reversal of rich and poor
column6: Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, and now their conditions are reversed; this shows status and present comfort do not settle the final account.

column5: steward reduces a debt by half
column6: The steward changes an oil debtor's bill from one hundred measures to fifty; unlike the commentary's condemned short measure, the parable places debt reduction inside a crisis strategy for future welcome.

column5: dishonest steward praised for prudence
column6: The master praises the dishonest steward's foresight, not his dishonesty; this complicates the commentary's pairing of financial manipulation and loss by distinguishing prudent use of wealth from moral accounting.

column5: preserving life leads to losing it
column6: Jesus says whoever seeks to preserve life will lose it, while whoever loses it will keep it; this gives a distinct saying in which self-protection reverses into the commentary's loss of self.

column5: former gains counted as loss
column6: Paul says the things that were gain to him he counted as loss for Christ; the accounting language directly meets the commentary's distinction between apparent assets and true profit.

column5: all things loss for the greater gain
column6: Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him; this adds a deliberate revaluation in which relinquishing worldly capital is itself gain.

column5: nothing brought in or carried out
column6: Paul says people bring nothing into the world and can take nothing out; this directly undercuts the assumption that accumulated wealth can secure the self.

column5: desire for riches plunges people into ruin
column6: Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and destructive desires; this connects pursuit of wealth to the commentary's loss of health, faith and self.

column5: stored wealth decays
column6: James says the rich person's wealth has rotted and garments have been eaten by moths; this gives physical form to the commentary's claim that capital can diminish while held.

column5: rust testifies against wealth
column6: Gold and silver rust becomes evidence against their owners and consumes them like fire; the verse links hoarding to a coming reckoning and adds a fire image to the commentary's crop-loss scene.

column5: joyful sale for a greater treasure
column6: The finder sells everything to buy the field with hidden treasure; this reverses the commentary's loss account by showing a total expenditure that is profitable because the acquired good is greater.

column5: work of faith and steadfast hope
column6: Paul remembers the community's work of faith, labor of love and steadfastness of hope; this is a specific Christian formulation of faith joined to action and endurance.

column5: faith without works is dead
column6: James says faith by itself, without works, is dead; this closely matches the commentary's neighboring exception, where belief is joined to righteous action.

column5: righteous live by faith
column6: In the vision's contrast between the proud and the upright, the righteous live by faith; this gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's group whose faith keeps them from loss.

column5: Paul rereads Habakkuk as gospel principle
column6: Paul quotes Habakkuk's righteous-by-faith line as the revelation of God's righteousness in the gospel; this Christian reading emphasizes faith as the principle of life alongside the commentary's fuller faith-and-deeds description.

column5: two ways, life and death
column6: The Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death; this gives a concrete early Christian form to the commentary's secondary sense of loss as leaving the right path.

column5: self, community and the urgency of now
column6: Hillel asks who one is if wholly for oneself and, if not now, when; the saying joins the commentary's isolated human, mutual counsel and finite time.

column5: do not separate from the community
column6: The Mishnah warns against separating from the community, trusting oneself until death, or postponing study until free; this connects collective support and urgency to the commentary's path out of isolation and loss.

column5: account before the Judge
column6: Akavya ben Mahalalel tells a person to know where he came from and where he goes, and before whom he will give account; this is a direct Jewish formulation of the commentary's human life reaching its reckoning.

column5: wealth redefined as contentment
column6: Ben Zoma asks who is rich and answers: one who rejoices in his portion; this challenges the commentary's market image by defining wealth through sufficiency rather than accumulation.

column5: one deed tips the moral scales
column6: The Talmud asks each person to see himself as balanced between merit and guilt, so one deed can tip himself and the world; this is a close rabbinic meeting of human action, scales and final consequence.

column5: people inscribed by their deeds at the New Year
column6: The Talmud describes books opened on the New Year and distinguishes the righteous, wicked and intermediate by their inscription for life or death; this gives the commentary's universal verdict and exception group a Jewish judgment-day framework.

column5: חסר (table sound correspondence; unverified)
column6: The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; the Hebrew speaker says לֹא אֶחְסָר, “I lack nothing,” within the shepherd's provision. The table's sound correspondence is unverified, and the verse supplies a precise counter-image of sufficiency.

column5: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
column6: The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Isaiah asks why anyone fears אֱנוֹשׁ, a mortal who dies and is like grass. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while the verse adds human mortality and fear.

column5: אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
column6: The source's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ is linked in the table to Hebrew אנש; Jeremiah calls his wound אָנֻשָׁה, incurable. This is the root's illness/weakness usage, not a claim that the Arabic noun means illness.
